Scientists just got closer to understanding the genetic roots of crime and its making them nervous

Nature was kind enough not to put up a paywall for this specific article: http://www.nature.com/tp/journal/v6/n9/full/tp2016155a.html

The researchers are right to be nervous. A diagnosis of ASPD is not proof that a defendant committed a crime, nor is the presence of these specific markers proof that a person has ASPD. Such an argument would go against everything our justice system is supposed to be about.

This is a great thing, though. Eventually, we will be able to edit these genes out of the gene pool using tools like CRISPR, and prenatal screening will give the parents the option to terminate a pregnancy when these genes are present.

The problem is we understand nothing at all all about the causality of genes. It's all completely and literally 100% correlations. For instance what if it is shown that a huge percentage of highly successful scientists also have similar genetic indicators? I expect the characteristic is also substantially overrepresented for politicians and successful businessmen, though I don't think too many would shed many tears if those types were literally removed from the gene pool. And perhaps that's not even the biggest concern. What if these genetic markets actually are not even related to ASPD and instead they just detected markers predictive of another sort of bias in the prison sampling?

Just skimming the paper this immediately pops up:

In a recent genome-wide association study (GWAS), Dick et al.10 found several markers with genome-wide significance associated with conduct disorder symptomatology, especially in the gene C1QTNF7, although none remained significant when individuals were classified dichotomously as cases and controls.

At the minimum that suggests various interplays we do not understand. And this sort of stuff is everywhere in every single thing related to genetics. The entire field is in my opinion one grand and overrated experiment in unforeseen consequences. I think a science without any sort of first principles cannot really be considered a science. I understand obviously that correlations can lead to principles, yet the field receives hype without context. As if we actually have a clear genetic understanding of ASPD or most of anything, which we do not. Designer babies... we don't even know which genes control hair color!

At the minimum that suggests various interplays we do not understand. And this sort of stuff is everywhere in every single thing related to genetics.

Only because we have very little data. This study had less than 1,000 subjects. If there are 1,000 genes that are about equally important in criminality, then the statistical power is almost nil. Come back when we have 10,000,000 subjects in the database.

The twin adoption studies are very clear that things like criminality are strongly driven by genetics. Also, we know from animal breeding experiments that personality is not just mostly genetic but can easily evolve. Some Russians turned viciously untameable fixes into housepets with 40 years of breeding.

Designer babies... we don't even know which genes control hair color!

Variants of MC1R are the most common source of red hair. Evolution seems to have strongly selected for them in Ireland, since the redheads there have at least half a dozen different variants. (If it were a genetic fluke in a common ancestor, there would be only one variant.)

Give it time. In no more than a decade or two it will be totally understood.

If you want something to really worry about, consider schizophrenia. The twin studies show that half of cases are due to the environment. Half! Is it a virus? Is it a fungal toxin in food? Could a schizophrenia bug strike down 10% of the population out of nowhere?

It's not about lack of samples size. You could have have a billion people and the exact same problem exists. The reason is the lack of causation. Genetics makes 0 effect to explain why a gene is attributed to certain characteristics, but simply that it is. It is correlations, not causations. The whole field of genetics is attributing correlations down to causation given a sufficient sample size but that is incredibly error prone, foolhardy, and subject to unforeseen consequences.

  • Geneticists make huge breakthrough!
  • We've determined the WAR GENE! We believe we can create world peace by simply disabling this gene which is present in 99.3% of all those who have instigated conflicts.
  • Shit shit shit! Turns out we accidentally just turned everybody female... and didn't stop war... Our bad.

Obviously this is an absurd example and it would be quite trivial to notice your "war gene" was actually mapping down to sex, yet the issue underlying it is not so absurd. Correlations are terrible for drawing causational conclusions from due to the constant presence of countless confounding variables. And they're even worse for acting on since without a causational understanding you are with near 100% certainty going to expose yourself to unforeseen consequences which may be immediately apparent or may take decades to manifest. Perhaps it only manifests in the offspring of the subject and not the subject itself. And they may manifest in 100% of subjects or they may manifest in 1 in a million subjects. These are very serious concerns that I think the general public is not aware of in relations to genetic engineering as the headlines always imply 100% causational understanding. And that is, I think, grossly irresponsible in a field that is already having a day to day impact in many peoples' lives.
